The pre-midterm defenestration of ACA enrollees looks like political madness – but the president appears to believe hitting poor people might work for him

Send us your questions on how the US economy is shaping the midterm elections

There is a manic quality to Donald Trump ’s desperate dash to do something, anything, ahead of November’s midterm elections to convince beleaguered Americans that he can make the pressures his policies have imposed on their livelihoods go away.

The US president offered to lower barriers against beef imports to limit surging meat prices, only to consider backtracking under pressure from the cow lobby. He offered to stop diesel exports, only to find oil companies were not interested . He weakened fuel efficiency standards, claiming this would trim the price of a new car (and forgetting to point out it will also raise spending on gas). In early October he started mailing $500 checks to nearly a million people touting his healthcare “wins”. Oh, and he promised adult Americans a $5,000 check if Republicans maintain control of Congress. That, too, will go nowhere .

In the face of such setbacks, maybe Trump felt he had to demonstrate he still can get something done. Still, it is somewhat counterintuitive that the administration, in the shape of Vice-President JD Vance, decided to broadcast the one initiative it did manage to bring to fruition: ejecting more than 750,000 enrollees from the Affordable Care Act (ACA) health insurance marketplaces, on grounds that they are not entitled to federal subsidies.

Trump could argue that the cuts fit within the administration’s promised commitment to restore fiscal discipline. But that part of the platform – which came as Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary, promised to trim the budget deficit to 3% of US gross domestic product – was never more than a rhetorical feint.

The pre-midterm defenestration of ACA enrollees by Trump’s “fraud taskforce”, by contrast, looks a lot like political madness, given the persistent economic anxieties articulated by Democratic and Republican voters across the country.

The savings from the ACA maneuver, estimated by the administration at $2.2bn per year, are chump change compared with the centerpiece of Trump’s fiscal policy – the One Big Beautiful Bill Act from 2025 that is expected to add $4.1tn to budget deficits over the next decade, largely due to tax cuts benefiting the most affluent Americans.

Pace Bessent, the budget deficit is growing rapidly, expected to rise to some $2tn in the fiscal year of 2026, roughly 6% of GDP and about 18% more than in fiscal 2024, the last year of the Biden administration.

Rather than stem budgetary red ink, it’s as if Trump’s objective is to spread misery beyond the 3 million Americans who had to drop their health insurance after the administration last year cancelled subsidies offered by the Biden administration.

The effort is something out of the playbook of Elon Musk’s Doge . His promise to rid the government of “waste” and “fraud” probably caused the deaths of millions of children in the developing world after the dismantling of USAID, but proved largely irrelevant to the task of saving money for the government. It may serve as a masterclass in trolling. But it is not a vote-winner.

Part of Trump’s brain seems to understand this. Trump paid in part for the “beautiful” bill’s colossal tax cut by cutting funding to Medicaid and the Snap food stamp program for low-income Americans. But he engineered most of the cuts to kick in after the midterms to minimize the political cost. The thinking was that lower-income Americans would happily vote for the Republicans out of gratitude for their somewhat bigger tax refund checks this year and tax breaks for overtime and tips (cleverly designed to expire at the end of Trump’s term) and not notice the cuts rushing down the pike on federal programs they relied on.

after newsletter promotion

But the new evictions from the ACA suggest that his brain’s darker side is winning. Indeed, it underscores Trump’s belief that hitting poor people might work for him. Rather than a commitment to sound fiscal policy, a helping hand for American families treading water or an economic platform of any kind, Trump’s latest exercise in “fraud prevention” points to a strategy revolving around punishing people he can define as “bad”. Deep underwater in the polls for his nutty stewardship of the economy, among other things, Trump seems to believe that his one remaining winning card is to do violence against constituencies that his base may not like. Top of the list are immigrants and low-income people. And so it is that ICE is also doubling down, announcing it will hire another 5,000 agents by the end of the year.

The president is on to something. About two-thirds of Republicans believe giving more aid to the poor does more harm than good, according to surveys from the Pew Research Center . Despite the repeated instances of abuse by federal agents, only 19% of Republicans think the Trump administration is doing too much to deport immigrants illegally in the country. The most radical rightwing voters are all in for federal deportations and don’t think the federal government should be responsible for ensuring Americans’ healthcare.

Perhaps Trump’s heart truly lies on the dark side. But doubling down on policies to please the most ardent fanatics in his base ultimately reveals the weakness of Trump’s position. Perhaps even he understands that he has lost the rest of the country . Punishing the poor and the foreign – alongside an unlikely $5,000 Hail Mary pass – is all he has left.

Burnham condemns Green Party's 'antisemitic' Zionism declaration

Published 14 October 2026, 14:39 BST

Andy Burnham has said he will not support his party forming a partnership with the Green Party as long as it maintains a policy of defining Zionism as a form of racism.

Speaking in the House of Commons, the prime minister said the motion, backed by Green members at its party conference earlier this month, was "wrong" and "antisemitic" and Labour would have "nothing to do with it".

The motion said Zionism was an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/ or domination of the non-Jewish population".

It was criticised by Jewish groups, as well as four Green MPs and two former leaders, one of whom said it was "dangerous" and "divisive".

Party leader Zack Polanski has said the motion was "imperfect" and that he had wanted to see it amended.

However, he has defended the substantial part of the motion arguing that "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by racist ideology" was "obvious". Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.

The motion, having been backed by members, has become party policy but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.

The subject was raised during Prime Minister's Questions, when Conservative MP Dame Harriett Baldwin urged Burnham to "rule out co-operating" with the Green Party.

Burnham replied: "Can I condemn the motion that was passed unequivocally.

"It is wrong, it is antisemitic, and this side of the House will have nothing to do with it.

"We will always take the right response when it comes to any partnerships we have with other parties.

"We cannot support a partnership with a party that holds the position that has recently been adopted."

In response to Burnham's comments, Polanski said: "I'm the only Jewish leader of a political party. I'm a victim of antisemitism every day and I've made it clear Jewish people are welcome in my party.

"You're a prime minister who arms a genocide and locks pensioners up for opposing it."

He added that the "blurring of challenging Israel and antisemitism" was "dangerous and irresponsible".

Labour is currently in coalition with the Green Party on local councils in Sheffield, Lewes and Warwick. In more than 10 other areas, Labour run the council with the Greens as part of a broader coalition.

A Downing Street spokesman would not confirm if the prime minister's position extended to local areas or just applied to national government level.

The adoption of the motion has prompted some Green Party figures to call for changes to the party's rules.

Last week, MP Ellie Chowns told the BBC: "I think it is clear that if we have policy, such significant and damaging policy, made by a vote of just 0.4% of our members, that something isn't working in our structures and our policy-making process."

Members of the Green Party of England and Wales endorsed the policy motion by 1,022 votes to 813 - a small fraction of the 230,000 members in the party.

Key backer of the motion Lubna Speitan has defended the motion arguing that it aimed to oppose "racist systems of oppression" adding: "We stand united against all forms of racism and discrimination - no exemptions."

True story about a former maths teacher who became a puzzle champion in retirement is squeezed into predictable sports-movie formula

I t’s not quite up there with Leonardo DiCaprio eating raw bison liver to get into character, but Michelle Yeoh reportedly spent two years learning the Rubik’s Cube to prepare for this Chinese drama in which she plays a real-life former maths teacher who became a champion in retirement. The true story is stretched and squeezed here, fictionalised to fit sports-movie formula; it ends up being so-so entertaining and funny in places, but disappointingly predictable. The biggest surprise is that cubing is so popular it has its own world championship.

Still, Yeoh gives a superb, spiky performance as blunt, foul-tempered Zhao Yanhong; following a stroke, Zhao is living in a nursing home where she is the resident badass, assaulting her robot care companion and making illicit trips to the off-licence. She discovers her natural talent for the Rubik’s Cube when a washed-up ex-champion called Wu Youwei (Haoran Liu) comes to the nursing home to give a tutorial. What follows is a classic sports-film structure, with qualifying heats and Zhao training day and night, lifting weights and pounding the city streets. (Yes, running is de rigueur in a Rubik’s Cube movie; physical strength is Zhao’s weak spot says Wu, who agrees to be her coach.)

Yeoh is enjoyably irascible as Zhao, who goes viral after thrashing a kid in her first competition. Her online fans call her “Grandma Zhao” and the film gently chips away at stereotypes of the older generation; fans assume Zhao is a cuddly elder, while younger cubers underestimate her skill and stamina. Yeoh brings intelligence to the role, but it’s odd that after making Zhao so testy and short-tempered, the film is all soft edges with a squishy centre. Next, can we expect a biopic of the six-year-old Chinese girl who recently set a Rubik’s Cube world record , solving it in just over four seconds?

stories.title: Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Man City chairman, deleted records show
stories.summary: The prime minister has been under growing pressure since the club was found guilty of Premier League rule breaches.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Man City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak (left) chats to Andy Burnham in 2019 at the Etihad Stadium, when he was mayor of Greater Manchester

Published 14 October 2026, 11:06 BST

Andy Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Manchester City football club's chairman while mayor of Greater Manchester, it has emerged.

The PM dined with Khaldoon Al Mubarak at matches in 2017 and 2018 - but this was not detailed in a statement on Monday by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) about his meetings with the club.

Burnham has been under pressure to clarify his previous discussions with Man City since the club was found guilty of having "systematically" broken Premier League rules, which it will appeal.

The PM, who was mayor until June, sparked widespread controversy when he said last month he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners now sold up.

On Monday, the GMCA released a statement about Burnham's meetings with Man City in his role as mayor for the region for almost a decade.

The statement said he had a formal meeting with Al Mubarak in October 2021 at the UK Government's Global Investment Summit, arranged by the Department for International Trade; and that he met the club chairman "informally in the stands" at a testimonial match in 2019 for former player Vincent Kompany.

It also said that "in his capacity as mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City at home matches on a small number of occasions".

But the statement did not specify that this referred to , external two hospitality dinners he had with the Manchester City chairman at separate matches.

A previous GMCA register of declarations for Burnham, seen by the BBC, detailed a "dinner with [then-Manchester City Council leader] Richard Leese and Chair of Man City" for an Everton match at the Etihad stadium in August 2017, valued at £300 for hospitality.

Below is another entry for "dinner with the Chairman at the Man City/Man Utd derby at the Etihad" in April 2018, valued at approximately £699.

Burnham previously declared those dinners, alongside a £150 pair of tickets to see Ed Sheeran perform at the stadium in May 2018.

But the register of declarations has since been deleted from the GMCA website, as first reported by The Sun. The BBC understands it is the authority's policy to only publish entries from the current mayoral term.

Man City guilty of 'sham' contracts and misleading accounts Published 29 September

BBC News has asked GMCA for more details about this policy - given its website has entries dating back to 2022, despite the current mayoral term beginning in 2024.

Downing Street has defended the two dinners with Man City's chairman, saying this was hospitality received at home games, which had been declared, rather than separate meetings with the club chairman.

But political pressure on Burnham to be clearer about any former discussions with Man City is continuing to mount.

Tory shadow sports minister Louie French said: "Andy Burnham promised the country and House of Commons full transparency on his dealings with Manchester City.

"This was essential after his inappropriate intervention into football."

And Reform UK's Robert Jenrick said "this saga stinks" as he accused Burnham of having apparently "concealed his extensive links to Man City's owners".

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has demanded for several days that No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club.

Burnham told the Rest Is Politics podcast last week he was "happy" to do this and would "quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as Mayor of Greater Manchester".

"None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021."

Asked at Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday whether anyone at the club had raised the charges they were facing with him or his team, Burnham said: "They did not raise those issues with me."

With the PM continuing to face pressure on the issue, he told MPs he was happy for "everything to be set out in full", referring to the GMCA's statement as "a full statement of my key dealings with the owners of Manchester City Football Club".

When asked by reporters why the statement did not refer to the two dinners, and what the difference is between "everything" and "key dealings", the PM's press secretary referred back to the GMCA statement.

The list of meetings, which was published by the GMCA on Monday, did not include detail on what was discussed. The BBC has asked GMCA why the two dinners were not specifically mentioned.

In September Man City - which has dominated the top flight of English football for years - was found guilty by an independent commission of breaching Premier League financial regulations.

The commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations.

Sanctions are yet to be announced and City, which denies any wrongdoing, has lodged an appeal against the verdict.

Earlier this month, Sir Richard Leese - who was head of Manchester City Council for 25 years until 2021 - defended a decade-old deal between the council and Man City owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG).

Under the partnership between the authority and the company, which is linked to the United Arab Emirates royal family, land was leased to ADUG at "below comparable rates", according to a University of Sheffield report.

stories.title: Why 'cool kids' won't let Swindon in Thames Valley
stories.summary: Why the "popular kids" in Oxfordshire are not letting Swindon in on the Thames Valley devolution deal.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Swindon leaders want the town included in the Thames Valley region

Published 14 October 2026, 06:31 BST

If you have ever been picked last for a sports team, or not invited to a party, you might know how the Borough of Swindon feels right now.

The government wants district and borough councils to be scrapped to make way for larger combined authorities, many of which will be run by mayors.

The issue for Swindon, however, is that some of the council leaders in Berkshire and Oxfordshire do not want Swindon to join them in a Thames Valley authority, arguing the geography does not work.

Swindon Borough Council leader Gary Sumner said: "It's like not being invited to the party with the popular kids."

The leader of Oxfordshire County Council Tim Bearder said: "With no offence to my friends in Wiltshire, you are not in the Thames Valley."

What is being proposed?

The government wants most areas of England to be under a mayoral authority, promising each area a greater say on how money should be spent as well as more power to unlock growth.

It means council areas being combined.

Under current plans Swindon would be included in the Thames Valley, which Sumner said would be good for the region.

"Swindon is a vast economic powerhouse in a potential Thames Valley devolution deal," he said.

"This is about coming together for growth we can pitch for infrastructure funds that can unlock investment in our town centre."

Conservative Sumner also said Swindon could help rural Oxfordshire councils reach a housing target under spatial development strategy , external by agreeing to allocate more land for housing in the town centre.

"Oxfordshire don't want their green fields covered in houses," he said.

"We've got brownfield sites that could deliver thousands and thousands of homes, at pace".

However, Bearder said: "It is not something you can use as a bargaining chip to get into a Mayoral authority."

Plans are stalling , with some council leaders arguing against Swindon being involved.

Swindon's high street would benefit from investment, said the council leader

Why don't they want Swindon?

"Perhaps they don't like the cut of Swindon's jib," said Sumner. "Perhaps they think they're too good for us.

"I'm really proud of our town and I'm upset when people think less of us and that's how it feels with two ends of the Thames Valley."

Windsor and Maidenhead council leaders also objected to the most recent plans, partly on the basis that a Foundation Strategic Authority was being proposed, instead of one run by a Mayor .

But on Swindon, Liberal Democrat Bearder said: "I don't think its a good fit. You would have to rearrange all the boundaries."

It is hoped under combined authorities, mayor and deputy mayors would also oversee things like the police and fire services - but currently Swindon's services operate in Wiltshire.

"It makes sense to have the set-up with Swindon staying in Wiltshire," Bearder said.

Meanwhile, Wiltshire Council leaders are looking to form a Wessex Mayoral Authority with nearby Somerset, Dorset and Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole.

Some leaders across Oxfordshire and Berkshire are keen on Swindon being involved.

Labour leader of Oxford City Council Susan Brown said it was "vital" Swindon was part of the Thames Valley.

"We're incredibly closely connected in terms of our economies," she said.

What happens now?

For a plan to be submitted to government, it needs approval from all parties across affected councils.

"It has to be unanimous and I will only do that when it is right," said Bearder.

Councils are waiting to hear what the next steps will be but elsewhere in the country local government reorganisation has been paused .

Sumner said he would continue to make the case for Swindon, hoping other leaders will have a change of heart.

"We need the Prime Minister to say, "If you want to see it happen, welcome Swindon," he said.

"This is the only thing that is going to get it across the line."

There are also discussions about whether or not Buckinghamshire and Milton Keynes would be part of the same group.

stories.title: Chris Mason: Lib Dems rally behind Davey as he pledges change
stories.summary: The BBC's political editor Chris Mason looks at the fallout from the Lib Dem frontbench resignations.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 14 October 2026, 06:11 BST

The Liberal Democrats don't tend to go for rhetorical fireworks or verbal kneecappings when grumbling about their leader.

But that doesn't mean there hasn't been grumbling going on. In the last week, two members of Sir Ed Davey's frontbench have resigned because they were unhappy with him, the party's direction and how policy is decided.

It meant the prospect of a lengthy and potentially testy meeting for Sir Ed with his MPs on Tuesday evening.

The Liberal Democrat leader arrived smiling, flanked by several loyal MPs, but made no comment as he entered the room.

Nearly four hours later, when the meeting broke up, his deputy Daisy Cooper said: "There is overwhelming support for Ed in the parliamentary party and a real sense that we need to come together as a group."

Earlier, behind closed doors, we understand Sir Ed told his MPs: "We have made changes. I am happy to embrace more changes. I want us to work as a united front." Another tacit nod to things being less than united recently.

In recent months he has appointed a new chief of staff, Ruth Younger, and James Holt, a veteran of the party's years in coalition government, as political director.

Last week's resignations were described to the BBC by one party figure as a rather Lib Dem insurrection – dissent expressed modestly.

Neither Charlie Maynard, a former Treasury spokesman and Alison Bennett, a former care and carers spokeswoman, have been publicly explicit about the reasons for their departures and both sought to express their concerns to Sir Ed privately and discreetly.

And, it is understood, there was no coordination between them in the timing of their resignations. They were departures that led to fury among some of their colleagues, irritated that it made the party look divided.

The resignations were the most clear indicators yet of an anxiety that has been bubbling away for over a year among some Liberal Democrat MPs. The essence of that anxiety is a fear they are not making enough of an impression and impact for the 72 MPs they have in parliament.

"The big frustration is the lack of cut through, being noticed. We are the biggest third party in the Commons in a century. But parliament doesn't shape things as much as it used to. It's about algorithms now," is how one figure put it.

They added: "In the world of social media there is an incentive, even a financial incentive, to be divisive and extreme. That's a sandpit we refuse to play in."

Nonetheless, the party is planning to up its social media game, but do so in line with what it sees as its authentic temperament and values.

Those around Sir Ed Davey privately acknowledge there is what they claim to be a "small group" of Lib Dem MPs who are not happy with his leadership. It is suggested that number isn't greater than "half a dozen" - a phrase used by several people we have spoken to.

But the anxiety about a perceived lack of impact involves far more MPs than that.

Some previous private critics have been won over by the recent changes to Sir Ed's team and are pleased to see the government talk about issues they care about: the European Union, changing the voting system for Westminster elections and social care in England, for instance.

They also hope the scale of their local campaigning, rather than poor national opinion poll ratings, will be more significant come the next general election.

Al Pinkerton, the party's Europe spokesman, told the BBC there had been a frank exchange of views during the meeting, but Sir Ed's willingness to make changes had been "very well received."

"It is a slog in the middle of a parliament, it's hard being the third party and it's such an enormous leap going from 15 MPs to 72," another party figure present told us. "But we're getting there putting in place the structures to better deal with that and keep MPs happy."

"Why would we get rid of our leader when no one else is pitching to be our leader? We need to let Ed get on with it," said another MP.

But they all know the underlying concern about impact – the challenge of being noticed – is real and not going away.

stories.body:
Fund upgrades UK’s GDP growth forecast for 2026 to 1.3%, but says it is likely to edge down next year

IMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’

John Healey should “stay the course” and continue repairing the UK’s public finances, the International Monetary Fund’s top economist has said, after the fund lifted its growth forecast for Britain.

Little more than a fortnight before Healey’s first budget, Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s economic counsellor, said the UK “stands out” among G7 countries in having a plan to narrow its deficit.

“The UK has already started a consolidation process,” she said. “The message for the UK is simply, stay the course.”

Tenreyro, a former member of the Bank of England’s monetary policy committee, was speaking at the launch of the IMF’s twice-yearly World Economic Outlook (WEO) at the fund’s annual meetings in Bangkok.

Healey is under pressure to announce a generous energy support package in the budget, before the sharp rise in energy bills expected in January .

But in its WEO report, the IMF advises member governments against across-the-board subsidies, saying any support should be “temporary, targeted and non-distortionary”.

In a fillip for the chancellor, who is due to arrive in Bangkok later this week, the IMF has upgraded its growth forecast for the UK this year, but it expects a modest slowdown in 2027 as higher energy prices take their toll.

Responding, Healey said: “Conflict in the Middle East and Europe is hitting people in the UK and around the world. But Britain’s economy is showing strong international resilience in the face of these challenges.”

The IMF predicted GDP growth of 1.3% for the UK this year, up 0.3 percentage points from its most recent update in July .

UK GDP growth has been stronger than expected in early 2026, at 0.6% in the first quarter and 0.5% in the second quarter. The Office for National Statistics has pointed to the strong expansion of AI-related businesses as one factor behind the upside surprise.

However, the IMF warned that prolonged high oil prices and rising interest rates meant growth was likely to “edge down” in 2027 “as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”.

It cut its UK growth forecast for next year modestly to 1.2%, from 1.3%.

Markets have been revising up their expectations of future inflation and interest rates across big economies since the Middle East conflict re-escalated in the summer.

The Bank of England’s nine-member monetary policy committee is now widely expected to raise the policy rate at its November meeting, echoing similar moves by the Federal Reserve , European Central Bank and Bank of Japan.

after newsletter promotion

Mortgage rates in the UK have already been rising in response to higher funding costs for banks in financial markets.

The BoE policymaker Megan Greene argued on Tuesday morning that the IMF’s growth upgrade was proof that UK interest rates should be higher.

Speaking to the Atlantic Council at the IMF meetings in Bangkok, Greene argued that interest rates were currently not very restrictive.

“There’s more recently been some labour market data that has also suggested that maybe slack in the labour market has peaked, so the labour market is loose,” Greene said.

The IMF singled out the UK as among the countries – also including Japan – where core inflation, which excludes volatile commodities such as energy, was not expected to return to the 2% target until late next year.

It expects average inflation in the UK to be 3.3% this year and to remain at 2.8% in 2027 – a challenge for Healey and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who are promising to offer voters a “breathing space” from rising costs.

Healey will spend little more than 24 hours in the Thai capital before flying home to put the finishing touches to his 28 October budget.

He is expected to focus on plans to devolve more tax revenues to mayoralties, alongside measures to help households cope with higher energy bills before the winter.

A string of other challenging decisions, including when the UK should be aiming to spend 3% of GDP on defence, is expected to be delayed until a big spending review at some point next year.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) warned this week that the budget would be a “work of fiction” unless Healey explained how he would deal with what it said were £35bn of future spending pressures.

ZyMix, which is being pushed on university campuses as the UK’s first super app designed “for gen Z”, combining chat, payments and community features, has a contract with a German-based subsidiary of Tencent Holdings, a Chinese conglomerate in Shenzhen.

Tencent Holdings was added in January 2026 to the US Department of Defense’s (DoD) list of Chinese military companies, which is formally known as the section 1260H list.

The citation on the DoD list says that the company, which is a gaming and social media conglomerate, is indirectly affiliated to the Chinese People’s Liberation Army.

The blacklist is part of a US attempt to counteract what it regards as Beijing’s efforts to increase its military power by using technology from Chinese firms, universities and research programmes.

The DoD is prohibited from entering into, renewing or extending contracts for goods, services or technology with any entity on the list although wider sanctions are not automatic.

A Tencent spokesperson said: “Tencent’s inclusion on this list is clearly a mistake. We are not a military company or supplier. Unlike sanctions or export controls, this listing has no impact on our business. We will nonetheless work with the Department of Defense to address any misunderstanding.”

China’s footprint in higher education in the UK has become a controversial issue. MI5 recently warned British universities to cut ties with the China General Technology Research Institute.

The domestic intelligence service claimed it was secretly channelling funding from Beijing’s intelligence apparatus to UK-linked academics to improve the technical espionage capabilities of China’s ministry of state security.

The link between the Chinese-owned infrastructure and ZyMix was initially disclosed in the company’s privacy policy at the time of its launch last week.

The document, which is legally required, said that Tencent (Frankfurt) stored user-generated content and messages. After the Guardian approached the company, the privacy policy was rewritten and mention of Tencent was removed.

The policy now states that users’ personal data is stored and processed primarily in the United Kingdom and the EU, adding that “some of our service providers are located in other countries, including the United States”.

It goes on to say that “auxiliary infrastructure providers, hosted in the EU, receive only encrypted user messages and limited technical data, such as technical statistics, licence validation when the app starts”.

A spokesperson said: “As a newly launched startup, we are updating our privacy notice as we develop our services, including clarifying that Tencent, Twilio and the other providers concerned are used solely for performance testing.”

The spokesperson added: “Our agreement is with Tencent Cloud Europe BV, which we use for auxiliary services, rather than as the provider that stores ZyMix user data. We take our obligations under UK data protection law seriously.”

The new privacy policy invites those who wish to know the identity of their suppliers to request the information from the company.

In response to a request from the Guardian, Tarique Ghaffur, a former assistant commissioner at the Metropolitan police, who described himself as a security consultant for ZyMix, responded.

He said: “We have reviewed your request as against our private privacy [sic] you mentioned. Unfortunately, at the present time for reasons of commercial confidentiality, contractual obligations and legal privileges, we are not able to provide you with the requested information.”

Fraser Sampson, a professor of security and national governance and formerly the UK’s biometrics and surveillance camera commissioner, said he was “sceptical when ‘commercial confidentiality’ arguments are used to duck basic policy questions and amending policy on the fly is never reassuring”.

He added: “When companies ask us for our personal data, they should expect us to ask them where it’s being kept, for what purpose(s) and who they’re going to share it with – and be prepared to answer fully.”

Sam Dunning, the director of the UK-China Transparency NGO, said: “There are serious questions about whether ZyMix have taken due care before launching this product.”

A spokesperson for ZyMix said: “Whilst still in its beta stage, the ZyMix app has been developed to fully comply with all UK data, privacy and financial regulations.”

ZyMix is heavily targeting the university market and is offering £200 to £400 a month to people who agree to be brand ambassadors on campuses. Staff roles have also been advertised in the UK by ZyMix for Mandarin-speaking applicants.

One advert on LinkedIn for the job of operations manager (Mandarin speaking) required “excellent written and verbal communication skills in both English and Mandarin (required for daily communication with the China team)”.

Separately, a distinct company appeared to be recruiting on behalf of ZyMix on WeChat, the Chinese instant messaging service, saying: “The product, R&D, design and testing team is in Greater China, with branch-company bases covering: Taipei / Shenzhen / Guangzhou / Hangzhou / Chengdu / Zhengzhou.”

Ghaffur said that Flicknmix, the UK company that publishes the ZyMix app, “does not have any subsidiaries or branch offices in China. Our aim is to create opportunities within the UK”. A spokesperson for ZyMix described it as “British born”.

EFF and the ACLU of Northern California represent SIREN and CAIR California, two non-profits that serve San Jose residents, in this case. Make no mistake: We believe this ruling is wrong on the law, and we will appeal. The ruling ignores the importance of landmark rulings from the U.S. Supreme Court regarding the invasiveness of aggregating collected data on an individual over time, including one issued just months ago . It also severely underestimates the harm that ALPRs cause, in San Jose and around the country. San Jose’s ALPR surveillance system is inescapable. It blankets the city’s streets in nearly five hundred cameras that continuously photograph every car that passes by and retains the collected data for a month or longer. In our briefs, we argued that law enforcement officers who warrantlessly search the resulting ALPR database are violating the California Constitution’s ban on unreasonable searches and its guarantee of privacy. The court disagreed, explaining that based on one California appeals court case involving individual streetlight cameras, people do not have a reasonable expectation of privacy when driving on a public road. This is wrong. Networked ALPRs are not individual streetlight cameras. Their net effect of tracking and mapping cars as they travel reveals patterns of life, intimate relationships, and much more. stories.title: Privacy's Defenders Podcast: No Privacy Without Encryption
stories.summary: When we communicate online today – from your personal emails and DMs to secure international commerce – we usually do so with encryption. Encryption converts readable data into unreadable gibberish to protect our privacy and security. This didn’t just happen organically. Three decades ago, the U.S government treated encryption like a weapon, and it took some unlikely heroes to set it free: a grad student, a junior lawyer, and a fledgling digital rights group who sued the federal government. The ruling in Bernstein v. Department of Justice held that code is speech and so is protected by the First Amendment – a precedent that underpins the internet as we know it today. This landmark case was led by Cindy Cohn, then a young pro bono lawyer working on behalf of EFF, who went on to become EFF’s legal director and then executive director. In this episode, Cindy – who left EFF in June – speaks with Dan Bernstein, who was a Cal Berkeley grad student when he developed a simple encryption algorithm called “Snuffle.” Because federal law classified encryption as a war munition, publishing Snuffle meant submitting it to the government for review, getting a license as an arms dealer, and being granted a license the government had no intention of granting.
